title: The Second Letter to the Thessalonians
lead: A short letter in the names of Paul, Silvanus and Timothy to the young church at Thessalonica, written to steady believers under persecution who had been told that the day of the Lord had already come. It promises God's just judgment, sets out what must happen first (the rebellion and the man of lawlessness), and orders the church to deal with members who refused to work. Whether Paul wrote it or a later follower wrote in his name is one of the most divided questions in the study of Paul's letters.

sections.b: It thanks God for the readers' growing faith under pressure and promises relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven (1:3-12); corrects the claim that the day of the Lord is already here by listing what must come first, the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness, who is now held back (2:1-12); thanks God for choosing them and urges them to hold to the traditions they were taught (2:13-17); and commands the church to keep apart from members who live out of line and will not work, while still treating them as brothers (3:6-15). It closes with a greeting in Paul's own hand (3:17).

The church received the letter as Paul's. Since J. E. C. Schmidt (1798) and William Wrede (1903) many scholars have argued that a later writer composed it, using 1 Thessalonians as a model: the wording follows 1 Thessalonians closely, the tone is cooler, signs before the end seem to clash with the thief-like suddenness of 1 Thessalonians 5:2, and the warning about a letter 'that seems to be from us' (2:2) with the stress on Paul's signature (3:17) can be read as a forger's self-defense. Wolfgang Trilling and Maarten Menken argue for a later writer; Abraham Malherbe and Charles Wanamaker defend Paul, Wanamaker even arguing that this letter came first. A 2011 survey of 111 scholars at the British New Testament Conference found 63 for Paul, 13 against and 35 unsure.
